mutations.because: the run never consults the lock at all, which is the mutation the row names for the lock. Every other guard in acquire_lock is defence in depth and deliberately redundant — the judgement refuses a live holder, the rename is arbitrated, the nesting of a candidate inside an existing lock is detected, and the read-back insists the name carries this run's own pid — so weakening any ONE of them still leaves an answer and still exits 75. Removing the call is the only way to show what the lock is actually for: with it gone, a second run starts beside a live holder, takes the same TMPDIR, refreshes and merges the same branches concurrently, and exits 0. Nothing in the script notices, because nothing is left to notice. The planted holder in the test is THIS test process's own pid, so the honest script must answer 75 and name it; the mutant instead merges PR #101 and deletes its branch on the forge

the check that the lock moved aside is the one that judged dead is the whole of the reclaim's safety, and the `mv` cannot do it alone: the rename is what arbitrates between two reclaimers, but it happily renames a LIVE run's lock out of the way when that lock replaced the dead one between this run's `ps` and this run's `mv`. With the comparison gone, the live lock is deleted, the name is free, and this run takes it and merges — while the run that was holding it merges too, still believing it holds the lock, and its release at exit declines to remove a name this run now owns. Two runs merge at once and both exit 0, which is the one outcome the lock exists to make impossible, and it is silent. The other lock tests cannot see it: the plain dead-pid test has no replacement to confuse it, and the live-holder test never reaches a reclaim. The test that sees it uses the MERGE_PRS_TEST_PAUSE_AFTER_LIVENESS hook to hold this run between the judgement and the `mv`, swaps in a lock carrying a LIVE pid, and then requires 75 plus that live lock still on disk

mutations.because: putting the worktree and the branch back into the marker is the regression this lane was sent back for, and it is one line: a worktree path may contain a space, so the moment the marker carries one again, the line stops being a line the caller can match whole. Here the caller matches with `grep -qx "MERGED $pr"`, so the extra fields make every match fail and a PR that merged is treated as one that did not — its worktree is never removed and its branch is never deleted on the forge, which is the silent half of a refusal. Under the old `read -r` parse the same marker was worse rather than better: it split into four fields, so a path like `/x/My Work/wt` became `/x/My` in WORKTREES and the rest in BRANCHES. The test is the one that merges a PR from a worktree whose path contains a space and then requires the worktree gone and the branch deleted, which is the only assertion in the file that can tell a marker carrying a path from one that does not

mutations.because: the reclaim then compares only the pid halves of the two tokens, which is the decision the nonce exists to overrule. A stale lock and the live lock that replaced it are then free to agree about the pid - which is the whole of what a stale lock and its replacement can be relied on to agree about, because the kernel recycles pids and hands a crashed holder's number to somebody else - and the mv that arbitrates between two reclaimers is perfectly happy to rename a LIVE run's lock out of the way and delete it. Both runs then merge, both exit 0, and the run whose lock was deleted never learns it had one. The nonce is what makes the two distinguishable, and trimming it off both sides of the comparison is exactly the regression. No other test can see it: the plain dead-pid reclaim has no replacement to confuse it, the live-holder test is refused before any reclaim, and the earlier race test swaps in a lock with a DIFFERENT pid, which a pid-only comparison already rejects. The test that sees it plants the same pid with a different nonce at the pause hook, and requires 75 with the replacement still on disk carrying its own nonce

mutations.because: one missing space, and the lock becomes unreclaimable for the rest of the host's life. Every reader takes the pid half with `${token%% *}`: a token written `$$-$$-<nonce>` has no space in it, so that expansion returns the WHOLE string, `1234-1234-99-1699…`, which is not `<->` — so the liveness branch is never entered, the run falls through to the `-d $LOCK_DIR` test, and answers 75. Forever, to every run, including the one that owns the crashed lock: nothing can ever judge it dead, and the nonce that would have made two tokens distinguishable is welded to the pid instead of separated from it. This shipped once already, and every test in the file agreed with it, because every reclaim test PLANTS a lock file and the harness wrote `<pid> <nonce>` — the documented shape, not the shape the script produced. That is why the test this mutation is aimed at exists: it starts a real run, lets the script's own acquire write the token, SIGKILLs the holder, and asks the next run to cope with what was actually written. It fails here on the format itself, before the reclaim is even attempted, which is the earliest the defect is visible at all

mutations.before:
for sweep in {1..20}; do
      kill -0 -- "-$group" 2>/dev/null || break
      kill -KILL -- "-$group" 2>/dev/null
      sleep 0.1
    done
mutations.because: removing the sweep leaves one TERM as the whole of the teardown, and a TERM is only ever enough for a process that handles it. Anything still answering in that group when the signal has been delivered and has done everything a signal can do — a `gh` or a tool that traps or ignores TERM, which is ordinary and not exotic — stays running, and the run then hands back a lock that a process is still sitting under. The next runner is told the host is free, takes the lock, and merges beside it: the exact failure the lock exists to prevent, arrived at from the other end. The loop is bounded and it comes BEFORE release_lock, which is the ordering the test asserts: it asks whether the process is dead at the moment the lock directory disappears, because a process still alive then is a process this run told the next one was not there. The survivor in the test ignores TERM outright, so the assertion cannot pass by luck and does not depend on how fast the signal arrives
command: a process the signal cannot kill
